title: Research Bite #24: A Marked Improvement? A Review of the Evidence on Written Marking
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #24 covers the Education Endowment Foundation and Oxford University's review "A Marked Improvement? A Review of the Evidence on Written Marking," commissioned to establish what the evidence actually supports across common marking practices -- grading, corrections, thoroughness, pupil response time, dialogue, targets, frequency, and speed. The headline finding is uncomfortable for a practice this central to teacher workload: the quality of evidence specific to written marking is low, with most existing studies small in scale or drawn from higher education and EFL settings rather than primary or secondary classrooms. Within that thin evidence base, a few practical distinctions do hold up -- careless mistakes and misunderstanding-driven errors likely need different responses, awarding a grade alongside comments can crowd out attention to the formative comments themselves, and marking has little effect unless pupils are given dedicated time to actually read and respond to it. The review's most quotable conclusion is that schools should mark less but mark better, prioritizing specific, actionable targets over exhaustive coverage of every piece of work. For teachers and school leaders under workload pressure, the review offers evidence-backed cover to scale back low-value marking practices like blanket acknowledgment marking in favor of fewer, more targeted interventions.
points: The uncomfortable headline finding that the evidence base specific to written marking is low quality and thin, despite marking's outsized role in teacher workload.

The distinction between careless mistakes (best marked simply as incorrect) and misunderstanding-driven errors (best addressed with hints or guiding questions) gives teachers an evidence-informed triage rule.
Marking has little effect on pupil progress unless dedicated time is set aside for pupils to actually engage with and respond to it -- feedback without response time is largely wasted effort.
The review's central recommendation -- to mark less but mark better -- reframes reducing marking volume as an evidence-aligned choice, not just a workload compromise.
quotes: This review of marking practices, commissioned by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), examines the evidence for a variety of marking approaches. The review notes a dearth of high-quality research in this area, particularly in primary and secondary school settings.
The quality of existing evidence focused specifically on written marking is low. Few large-scale, robust studies have examined marking practices.

Teachers should differentiate between careless mistakes and errors resulting from misunderstanding. Errors resulting from misunderstanding may be best addressed by providing hints or questions that lead pupils to underlying principles.
Awarding grades for every piece of work may reduce the impact of marking, particularly if pupils become preoccupied with grades at the expense of considering teachers’ formative comments.
Pupils are unlikely to benefit from marking unless some time is set aside to enable pupils to consider and respond to marking.
A mantra might be that schools should mark less in terms of the number of pieces of work marked, but mark better.

A 2016 report from the Independent Teacher Workload Review Group suggested that providing written feedback on pupils’ work has become disproportionately valued by schools, and the quantity of feedback has too often become confused with quality.
